analysis.one_liner: Forces public disclosure of automakers' safety defect data, boosts safety fines, and restricts agency-industry revolving door.
analysis.headline: The Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 2014 was introduced by a single Democratic senator with no cosponsors, sent to the Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require automakers to hand over safety defect reports — complaints, recalls, warranty claims — and make most of that data public. It would raise maximum fines for safety violations fivefold, give regulators power to force immediate recalls when a defect is an imminent hazard, and require dealers to disclose unremedied defects to used-car buyers. It would also bar former safety regulators from representing carmakers for two years, impose a per-vehicle fee on manufacturers to fund the safety agency, and raise the agency's annual funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and passengers, especially used-car buyers who would get written notice of unremedied defects before purchase. The general public also gains from a safety agency with more funding, stronger fines, and data it can search itself.

how_it_helps.text: Requires automakers' early warning data on possible defects — recalls, complaints, warranty claims, field reports, technical service bulletins — to be publicly disclosed, with a presumption in favor of maximum public availability, instead of being kept confidential.

Raises the maximum civil penalty for violating federal motor vehicle safety requirements from $5,000 to $25,000 per violation and eliminates the cap on total penalties for a related series of daily violations.
Requires the Secretary of Transportation to order immediate owner notification and remedy when a defect presents an imminent hazard of serious injury or death.
Bars dealers from selling or leasing a used car without telling the buyer in writing about any unremedied safety defects and getting the buyer's written acknowledgment.

Prohibits NHTSA safety officials from representing regulated manufacturers before the agency for two years after leaving, and penalizes manufacturers that hire them, including a civil penalty of at least $100,000 plus 90% of the individual's compensation.

Funds NHTSA's safety work through a new Vehicle Safety Fund financed by a $3-to-$9-per-vehicle fee on manufacturers, and raises authorized NHTSA appropriations from about $98 million to $200-$280 million per year.

analysis.who_pays: Motor vehicle manufacturers pay the per-vehicle safety fee, higher potential penalties, and compliance costs from public disclosure of defect data. Used-car dealers bear new disclosure paperwork and liability for selling vehicles with known unremedied defects.

drawbacks.text: The per-vehicle safety fee on manufacturers would likely be passed into vehicle prices, and authorizing a dedicated fee stream could arguably reduce Congress's oversight over how NHTSA is funded.

Mandatory public disclosure of defect reports and the $25,000-per-violation penalty structure could raise manufacturers' costs and encourage more defensive, high-volume reporting, which critics of early warning disclosure have said may bury real signals in noise.
The used-car disclosure mandate imposes obligations on dealers and limits on auctions unless the Secretary exempts them, adding compliance costs to a low-margin business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to the public: visible defect data, faster recalls of imminent hazards, disclosures before used-car sales, and a better-funded safety regulator. The costs fall on manufacturers and dealers and are modest relative to vehicle prices — the fee tops out at $9 per car in year three — while the higher penalties only bite when firms actually violate safety rules. The main good-faith concern is disclosure quality and who ultimately pays the fee, not a serious public downside.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced by one senator with zero cosponsors, referred to the Commerce Committee on day one, and left there until the Congress expired — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Sen. Rockefeller introduced the bill on June 26, 2014, near the end of the 113th Congress.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day, and no further action was ever taken.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers are better off because the bill never advanced: defect data stays confidential, penalties stay at the old $5,000 level, the per-vehicle fee never materializes, and the revolving-door restriction never takes effect. Used-car buyers, however, have since gotten some disclosure protections through separate recall-notice rules — though not from this bill.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (sponsoring senator)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 2014; as committee chair he had authority to advance it but did not schedule a markup before leaving office.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by the bill's own sponsor
against.what_they_did: Took no action: no hearing, no markup, no vote on the bill after its referral on June 26, 2014.

against.name: Auto manufacturers and dealers (implied opposition)
against.role: Regulated industry with a stake in defeating the bill
against.what_they_did: The bill targeted manufacturers and dealers with fees, higher penalties, public disclosure, and disclosure mandates; no evidence of the industry's lobbying on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no party split can be measured; the bill died with a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: Automakers would have paid a new per-vehicle user fee, faced fivefold higher civil penalties with no cap on serial violations, and lost confidentiality over defect complaint data that could fuel recalls and lawsuits. Bill text and the CRS summary make all three mechanisms explicit.

Dealers selling 10 or more vehicles a year would have had to disclose unremedied safety defects in writing before any sale or lease, creating compliance costs and liability for vehicles sold with known defects. There is an escape hatch when recall data is not accessible or the defect is fixed before delivery.

industries.industry: Vehicle safety regulatory sector (former NHTSA officials)
industries.note: The bill's two-year revolving-door ban would have cut off a lucrative path by which former agency officials move to the companies they regulated, with civil penalties for the officials and the firms that hire them. Ordinary drivers benefit when regulators do not owe their next job to industry.

industries.industry: Auto industry trade groups and lobbying apparatus
industries.note: The bill did not pass, so no change to industry's position occurred; its defeat leaves existing confidentiality practices, penalty levels, and funding arrangements in place. The bill never reached a hearing, so it never threatened these arrangements.
